items.prompt: Explain why a business needs its cost information to be accurate.
items.canonical_answer: Because four decisions run on it: what to charge, what to keep making, where spending is drifting from plan, and whether performance is improving. A wrong figure can mislead any of those decisions that depends on it materially, and the direction depends on which way the figure is out. Understated, a product looks profitable, so it is priced low and pushed, and the business loses money faster. Overstated, it looks like a failure and may be dropped, while any cost it was helping to cover that would be incurred anyway stays behind. Because a shared total is divided between products, the same allocation usually does both at once - too little on one product means too much on another.
marking_guidance: Reason: a wrong cost figure can mislead any decision that materially depends on it.
Direction: must condition the error on whether the cost is understated or overstated, not assert a single common direction.
Purpose: the answer must say why, not only what.
Reward at least one named decision that depends on the figure, developed through one correct pathway.

items.prompt: Explain how inaccurate cost information can lead a business to stop making a product that was worth keeping.
items.canonical_answer: A product is charged with more of the shared costs than it would carry under a different basis, so its recorded cost per unit is overstated and it shows a loss. On that figure the business stops making it. The sales and the contribution from that product go. The shared costs do not, so far as they are unavoidable - a rent fixed by a lease, or salaries that do not fall with output, are unchanged and now fall on the products that remain. Those products' costs rise in turn, so the business ends with less contribution, the same unavoidable overheads, and a second product that now looks unprofitable. The chain only reaches that ending for the part of the cost that would have been incurred anyway: whatever would genuinely have disappeared with the product is saved and has to be set against the contribution lost. Whether that ending is the wrong one also depends on what the freed capacity does next: if the resources the dropped product used can earn a larger contribution on something else, stopping it was right despite the overhead staying behind.
marking_guidance: Condition: the shared costs are divided using a chosen basis, and the part that stays behind is the part that is unavoidable.
Mechanism: an overstated share makes a viable product show a loss.
Consequence: the contribution is lost while the unavoidable overhead stays and is redistributed.

Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the profit of the business and the apparent cost of the remaining products, and must not treat the lost contribution as the whole effect without asking what the freed capacity would earn.

items.prompt: A guesthouse in Swakopmund charges the same nightly rate all year and does not separate the cost of running its restaurant from the cost of the rooms. Explain one decision it cannot make well without better cost information.
items.canonical_answer: It cannot tell whether the restaurant is worth running. Its costs - kitchen staff, food, the share of electricity and cleaning - are mixed in with the rooms, so the guesthouse knows only what the whole business spent. Without separating them it cannot say whether the restaurant covers what it costs, whether it is subsidised by the rooms, or what it would save by closing it and serving breakfast only.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between classifying a cost as fixed or variable and classifying it as direct or indirect.
items.canonical_answer: They answer different questions about the same cost. Fixed or variable asks what happens to the cost when output changes: a fixed cost stays the same over a period, a variable cost moves with output. Direct or indirect asks whether the cost can be traced to one product: a direct cost belongs wholly to one product, an indirect cost has to be divided up. Because the questions are separate, a cost can be both direct and fixed - the salary of a supervisor who works on one product line only.
marking_guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required.
Boundary: behaviour as output changes versus traceability to one product, and the consequence must be stated.
Reward the point that a cost can be direct and fixed at the same time.

items.prompt: Kaoko Juice pays N$96 000 a month in rent, insurance and permanent staff salaries whatever it produces, and spends N$16 on fruit, a bottle and a label for each bottle it makes. Explain the difference between its fixed costs and its variable costs.
items.canonical_answer: A fixed cost does not change with output over the period; a variable cost changes directly with output. Kaoko's N$96 000 is fixed for the month: it is the same at 8 000 bottles as at 12 000. The N$16 a bottle is variable: 12 000 bottles need N$192 000 of materials and 8 000 bottles need N$128 000. The consequence is that fixed cost per bottle falls as output rises - N$8 a bottle at 12 000, N$12 a bottle at 8 000 - while variable cost per bottle stays at N$16.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - whether the total changes when output changes over the period.

2 marks (AO2): applied to Kaoko - the N$96 000 is the same at any output this month, while the N$16 a bottle is spent again on every bottle made, so fixed cost per bottle falls as output rises; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: how the cost behaves when output changes, not what the cost is called.

items.prompt: Explain why the average cost of a unit usually falls as a business produces more.
items.canonical_answer: Because the fixed costs do not rise with output. The rent, insurance and salaries are the same total whether the business makes 100 units or 1,000, so as output rises that total is carried by more units and the fixed cost per unit falls. The variable cost per unit does not change, so the average cost of the whole unit falls with it. Nothing has become cheaper - the same rent is simply being shared out more widely.
marking_guidance: Reason: the same fixed total is spread over more units while variable cost per unit is unchanged.
Purpose: the answer must say why, not only what.
Do not accept 'buying in bulk' alone as the mechanism; the question is about spreading fixed costs.

items.prompt: A workshop has fixed costs of N$54 000 a month and variable costs of N$220 per unit. Calculate its total cost and its average cost per unit in a month when it makes 600 units.
items.canonical_answer: Total cost = fixed costs + (variable cost per unit x output) = N$54 000 + (600 x N$220) = N$54 000 + N$132 000 = N$186 000. Average cost = total cost / output = N$186 000 / 600 = N$310 per unit. The average is well above the N$220 variable cost because each unit is also carrying N$90 of fixed cost.
marking_guidance: Formula: total cost = fixed costs + (variable cost per unit x output).
Substitution must be shown, not only the answer.
Units: the currency or unit must appear on every figure.
Interpretation: one sentence saying why average cost exceeds variable cost per unit.

items.prompt: Why is it wrong to say that a fixed cost never changes?
items.canonical_answer: Because fixed means it does not change *with output*, within a range and for a period - not that it is permanent. A landlord can raise the rent. And when a business outgrows its premises it takes a second unit, at which point the rent steps up to a new level where it is fixed again. A business planning a large increase in output cannot assume its fixed costs will stay where they are.
marking_guidance: Reason: the answer must say why the belief is wrong, not only that it is.
Reward the point that fixed costs are fixed only within a range of output and a period.

items.prompt: An Okahandja workshop makes chairs and tables in one rented building. It buys N$450 of wood for each table and pays N$18 000 a month in rent. Explain the difference between a direct cost and an indirect cost for the workshop.
items.canonical_answer: A direct cost can be traced in full to one product; an indirect cost is incurred for the business as a whole and has to be divided between products before any of it can be charged to one. The N$450 of wood is a direct cost of a table: it goes into that table. The N$18 000 rent is indirect: chairs and tables share the building, so the share a table carries depends on the basis chosen to divide it - floor space, hours worked or units made. The consequence is that the table's direct cost is measured, whereas its share of the rent is a judgement.

2 marks (AO2): applied to the workshop - the wood traced to each table against the rent shared by chairs and tables, whose share depends on the basis chosen; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: traceable to one product against shared by several, with the consequence that one is measured and the other divided by judgement.

items.prompt: Explain one problem a business may have when allocating indirect costs to its products.
items.canonical_answer: The basis has to be chosen rather than measured. Floor space, machine hours, labour hours and units produced are all defensible, and they give different answers from the same real spending - a product occupying most of the floor but few of the machine hours carries a large share on one basis and a small share on the other. The problem is that the resulting cost per product is then used to decide whether to keep making it, so a choice about arithmetic can drive a decision about the business.
marking_guidance: Reason: the basis of apportionment is chosen, so the resulting product cost is a judgement.
Purpose: the answer must say why, not only what.

items.prompt: Explain how the way a business shares out its overheads can make a product look unprofitable when it is not.
items.canonical_answer: The business picks a basis for dividing the overheads - say floor space. A product that takes a lot of space but little machine time is charged with a large share. Added to its direct costs, that share pushes its recorded cost above its selling price, so it shows a loss. That recorded loss is an accounting result, not the effect of stopping: the product still sells for more than the cost of making it, so it is still contributing towards overheads the business would pay anyway. If the business acts on the recorded figure and drops it, the contribution goes while the unavoidable part of the overhead stays, so the business is worse off by the difference - unless enough of the overhead would disappear with the product, or the capacity it used could earn more on something else.
marking_guidance: Condition: overheads are divided on a chosen basis, and the overhead that stays behind is the part that would be incurred anyway.
Mechanism: a large share pushes recorded cost above selling price.
Consequence: the product shows an accounting loss that is not the incremental effect of stopping.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the profit of the business if the product is dropped, and must not treat the allocated loss as the cash effect.

items.prompt: A packaging firm makes boxes in three sizes on the same machines, in the same building. Explain one difficulty it faces in deciding how much of the factory rent each box size should carry.

Large boxes use more space and more machine time per box but are made in smaller numbers, so a per-box basis gives them a small share and a machine-hours basis a large one. Whichever it chooses decides which box size looks profitable, and there is no measurement that settles it.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between full costing and contribution costing.
items.canonical_answer: Full costing assigns all of a business's costs to its products; contribution costing assigns only the variable costs and holds fixed costs back as a cost of the period. The boundary between the methods is therefore fixed against variable, not direct against indirect. A supervisor employed on one line only is direct and fixed, so her salary is inside that line's full cost and outside its contribution cost. Power shared between several products is indirect and variable, so both methods charge it to products - though it must be divided between them first, which is why contribution costing reduces apportionment rather than removing it.
marking_guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required.
Boundary: fixed against variable is what separates the methods, and the consequence must be stated.
Do not reward 'fixed and indirect' treated as a single category.
Reward a direct-fixed or variable-indirect example.

items.prompt: A manufacturer with three product lines finds that one shows a loss under full costing. Evaluate whether it should use the full costing figure to decide whether to stop making that line.
items.canonical_answer: It should not decide on that figure alone. Two questions decide it, and the full-costing loss answers neither. The first is how much of the cost in that loss would actually disappear if the line stopped. The recorded loss includes a share of overheads divided on a chosen basis; where those overheads continue regardless, stopping the line removes its contribution and leaves the costs behind, so the business ends up worse off and the remaining lines look less profitable in turn. The second is what the freed capacity would earn. Positive contribution shows what is lost by stopping and replacing the line with nothing; if the plant, space and labour it uses could carry a product contributing more, stopping is right even though the overhead stays. The strongest argument for acting on the figure is that a line failing to cover its full share indefinitely is being carried by the others, and a business cannot carry it forever. On balance the decision should rest on avoidable cost measured against the best alternative use of the capacity, not on the allocated figure. The judgement changes if a real cost would go with the line - a warehouse that could be given up, a supervisor employed only on it - or if a better use of the capacity appears.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation is required, not a balanced list.
Context: the answer must be argued for a business whose overheads are shared across three lines.
Criterion: the decisive test is the contribution lost against the cost avoided AND the best alternative use of the capacity freed.
Counterargument: must acknowledge that a line permanently carried by the others is a real problem.
Condition: must name what would change the judgement - avoidable fixed costs, or a better use of the capacity.

If the business reads that as a second failing product it can repeat the mistake. Had the product had its own dedicated line or supervisor, part of the overhead would have gone with it and the chain would be weaker.

items.canonical_answer: Because the fixed costs of the period have to be paid whether anything is sold or not. In the opposite case, a product in a crowded market carries a price the market will not accept, and it does not sell at all. items.prompt: Analyse the risks a business takes when it accepts a special order at a price below its normal one.
items.canonical_answer:
The first risk is in the arithmetic rather than the market: the price has to beat every cost the order itself causes, not just the variable cost per unit. A run that needs a setup, a delivery or an hour of overtime carries those costs too, and an order that looked profitable on variable cost alone can lose money once they are counted. The second is the capacity: if demand rises while the order is being produced, the capacity it occupies would have earned the full contribution rather than the reduced one.

Then the market risks. The order is priced separately but the market is not. Existing customers paying the full price may learn what the special customer paid, and once they do they have a reason to ask for the same terms; refusing risks the relationship and agreeing loses margin across the whole order book. The special customer, having bought once at the lower price, treats it as the price. None of these is certain - a genuinely one-off order into a separate market may never become visible - but each is a way the contribution the order earns can cost more than it brings in.
marking_guidance: Condition: an order is accepted below the normal price.
Mechanism: incremental costs the order causes may exceed the variable cost per unit, and the lower price may become known or expected.
Consequence: the order can lose money, or margin is lost on other sales, or full-price capacity is displaced.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the profit of the business beyond the order itself.

items.prompt: A bakery sells bread rolls to cafes at N$14 a roll. Its total variable cost is N$5 a roll, including oven energy and every other input that rises with output. The baker is on a fixed monthly salary that does not change with output. The oven stands idle three mornings a week, with capacity for 1 200 rolls a morning and no other work waiting, and filling an idle morning creates no setup, overtime or other extra fixed cost. A hotel offers 900 rolls a week at N$9.80 a roll for a fixed three-month term, collected from the bakery, over which the bakery's costs and capacity are unchanged. Evaluate whether the bakery should accept.
items.canonical_answer: It should accept the three-month term as offered, and not extend it without deciding again. The decisive criterion is the incremental comparison: the total cost these rolls cause is the N$5 a roll of variable cost, because that figure already includes oven energy and every other input that rises with output, the baker's salary does not change, the hotel collects so there is no delivery cost, the order creates no setup or overtime, and 900 rolls fit inside a single idle morning's 1 200 with no full-price work displaced. At N$9.80 each roll leaves N$4.80, so 900 rolls add N$4 320 a week that the bakery would not otherwise have. The strongest argument against is that even three months of repeat supply is the kind of arrangement that becomes known to the cafes paying N$14, and that is hard to withdraw once the hotel has built it into its plans. That is why the fixed term matters: it keeps this an incremental decision over a period in which the capacity and the fixed costs really are unchanged, rather than a standing discount whose price would have to cover the whole business. The judgement changes if full-price demand grows into those mornings, because the capacity would then be earning N$9 a roll rather than N$4.80, or if the order grew beyond what the idle capacity holds and overtime had to be paid.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation is required, not a balanced list.
Context: must use the N$14, N$5 and N$9.80 figures, the fixed salary, the collection, and the 1 200-roll capacity.

Criterion: the comparison must be against the total cost the order causes, which the stem gives as the N$5 total variable cost with no extra fixed cost, and must confirm that no full-price work is displaced.
Counterargument: must address the standing nature of the order and the cafes paying full price.
Condition: must state what would change the judgement, including that a renewal beyond the stated term is a fresh decision and not the same incremental test.

items.prompt: Analyse the benefits to a business of using break-even analysis.
items.canonical_answer: It converts a plan into a number the business can act on. Knowing that 4 200 loaves a month is the break-even point turns a vague intention into a target every person in the bakery can be measured against, which is a different kind of instruction from 'sell more'. Knowing the margin between that figure and expected sales tells the owner how much room there is before a bad month becomes a loss, so the risk of the plan can be described rather than felt. And because the calculation is quick, a proposed change - a price rise, a cheaper supplier, higher rent - can be tested on paper before any commitment is made, which is far cheaper than discovering the effect afterwards. The value of all three depends on the figures being reasonable estimates; the technique sharpens a plan, it does not validate one.
marking_guidance: Condition: a business has estimates of its price, variable cost and fixed costs.
Mechanism: the calculation converts those into a target, a margin and a testable model.
Consequence: the business can set targets, describe its risk and test changes before committing.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the objectives of the business and the quality of its decisions.

items.prompt: Evaluate the usefulness of break-even analysis to the owner of a new coffee shop preparing a business plan.
items.canonical_answer: It is useful to her, and most useful for the plan itself rather than for what will actually happen. The decisive criterion is that she has no trading history: every figure in her plan is an estimate, and break-even analysis is the tool that turns those estimates into the one number that matters - how many cups a day she must sell before she earns anything. It also gives her lender something concrete to judge. The strongest argument against relying on it is that its answer is only as good as the estimates behind it, and a new business is exactly the case where those are weakest: she does not know her real footfall, her wastage, or whether her price will hold. The judgement holds provided she treats the figure as a target to test against reality in her first months, and recalculates once she has actual costs rather than guesses.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation is required, not a balanced list.
Context: the answer must turn on this being a new business with no trading history.
Criterion: the decisive test is what the technique gives someone with only estimates.
Counterargument: must acknowledge that estimates are weakest in exactly this case.
Condition: must state the condition - recalculating on real figures.

items.prompt: A hair salon calculates a break-even level of 240 haircuts a month and expects to do 300. Explain what the break-even figure tells the owner about her first month.
items.canonical_answer: It tells her that at 240 haircuts a month the salon's revenue exactly covers its total cost - the rent, the electricity and the chair rental are paid and the business makes neither a profit nor a loss. Every haircut after the 240th adds its contribution to profit. Against an expectation of 300, that is a margin of safety of 60 haircuts: sales can fall by 60 before the salon is back at break-even, and a quiet month of 230 puts it into a loss. How much profit those 60 haircuts represent cannot be worked out from these two figures - that needs the contribution per haircut, which the break-even output does not give her. What the figure does tell her is that the margin is thin, so she needs to know early in the month whether she is on pace.

Reasoning: the mechanism is that fixed costs are covered before profit begins.
Quantity: 60 is a margin of safety in haircuts, not an amount of profit; profit is a currency amount and cannot be calculated without contribution per haircut.

items.prompt: Analyse how a business can lower its break-even level of output.
items.canonical_answer: There are three levers and each acts on a different part of the same formula. Raising the selling price increases contribution per unit, so the fixed costs are covered by fewer units - though the calculation assumes the same volume still sells at the higher price, and if customers leave the business can end up further from break-even rather than nearer. Cutting the variable cost per unit raises contribution the same way, through cheaper inputs or less waste, and does not depend on how customers react - though it can cost quality if the saving comes from a cheaper input. Cutting fixed costs works directly on the numerator, but they are usually the slowest to move and cutting them can remove capacity the business needs if it grows. Which lever fits depends on which one the business can pull without damaging the others.
marking_guidance: Condition: the business wants to break even at a lower output.
Mechanism: each lever acts on contribution or on fixed costs.
Consequence: break-even output falls, with a different side-effect in each case.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the objectives of the business and the risk attached to each lever.

items.prompt: A bakery with a break-even output of 4 200 loaves a month is considering raising its price by N$2 a loaf to bring that figure down. Evaluate whether it should.
items.canonical_answer: It should not do it on the break-even figure alone. The decisive criterion is what happens to volume: the calculation showing a lower break-even holds the number of loaves constant, and that is precisely the assumption a price rise puts in question. If the bakery loses more than a small share of its customers, it will be selling fewer loaves against a lower break-even point and may be no better off, or worse. The strongest argument for the rise is that bread buyers are often loyal to a nearby bakery and a N$2 change is small in absolute terms, so the volume loss may well be minor - and the improvement in contribution is certain while the loss is not. The judgement turns on evidence the arithmetic cannot supply: what happened last time it raised prices, and what the nearest competitor charges. If neither is known, a trial in one shop is a cheaper way to find out than a permanent change everywhere.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation is required, not a balanced list.
Context: the answer must turn on the bakery's own volume response, not on the arithmetic.
Criterion: the decisive test is whether volume holds at the higher price.
Counterargument: must give the genuine case for the rise, not a token one.
Condition: must name the evidence that would settle it.

items.prompt:
On the break-even chart below, the revenue line rises more steeply than the total cost line. Explain what the difference between the two slopes represents, and use the chart to identify what it is here.

```
N$000        TR = total revenue      TC = total cost      FC = fixed costs
  480 |                                                    ***
      |                                                ****
  400 |                                           *****  +++++
      |                                       ****+++++++
  320 |                                ++**X**++
      |                       +++++++****
  240 |              +++++++++  *****
      |     +++++++++       ****
  160 |+++++-----------*****----------------------------------
      |            ****
   80 |       *****
      |   ****
    0 |***
      +---------+--------+--------+--------+--------+--------+>
      0       1 000    2 000    3 000    4 000    5 000    6 000  units
```

*Key: `*` is total revenue (TR), `+` is total cost (TC), `-` is fixed costs (FC), and `X` marks where TR and TC meet. All three lines are straight. TR passes through the origin; TC starts on the vertical axis at the level of the fixed cost line. Read values off the gridlines.*
items.canonical_answer: The revenue line rises by the selling price for every unit and the total cost line by the variable cost per unit, so the difference between the slopes is the contribution per unit. Reading the chart: revenue reaches N$480 000 at 6 000 units, so the price is N$80 a unit; total cost rises from N$160 000 at zero output to N$400 000 at 6 000, so the variable cost is N$240 000 / 6 000 = N$40 a unit. The difference is N$40, and that is why the vertical gap between the lines widens by N$40 for every extra unit - below 4 000 units it is a shrinking loss, above it a growing profit.
marking_guidance: Comparison: the two slopes must be compared, not read separately.
Interpretation: the answer must say what the difference means - it is the contribution per unit, and it sets how fast the profit gap widens. The figure must be derived from the chart.

items.prompt: Two businesses each sell 10 000 units a month and each trades above break-even. One earns N$380 contribution a unit, the other N$40. Analyse why the same fall of 1 000 units affects them differently.
items.canonical_answer: Every unit sold above break-even adds its whole contribution to profit, and every unit lost takes its whole contribution away, because the fixed costs do not move. Losing 1 000 units therefore costs the first business 1 000 x N$380 = N$380 000 and the second 1 000 x N$40 = N$40 000 - the same volume change, nearly ten times the swing in profit. That is a statement about the size of the swing, not about which business is closer to a loss: whether either falls into loss depends on its margin of safety and how large its fixed costs are, and a high-contribution business with a wide margin can absorb the fall comfortably while a low-contribution one with a narrow margin cannot.
marking_guidance: Condition: both businesses sell the same volume and trade above break-even, with fixed costs unchanged.
Mechanism: each unit gained or lost carries its whole contribution.
Consequence: the same absolute volume change moves profit further for the higher-contribution business.
Objective or stakeholder: must reach the profit swing, and must NOT infer proximity to loss from contribution per unit alone - that depends on margin of safety and fixed costs.

items.prompt: One business has a margin of safety of 500 units and another of 5 000 units. Explain whether the second is necessarily safer.
items.canonical_answer: Not necessarily - the comparison has to be against the size of each business. If the first sells 1 000 units a month, its 500 is half its output and sales could halve before it lost money. If the second sells 100 000, its 5 000 is 5%, and a small fall puts it into loss. Expressed as a percentage of current output the first business is far safer, which is why the percentage is the more useful form when comparing two businesses of different sizes.
marking_guidance: Comparison: each margin must be compared against its own business's output, not against the other margin.
Interpretation: the answer must say what the figure means - the percentage form is what makes two businesses comparable.

items.prompt: Kaoko Juice sells 12 000 bottles a month at N$28. Its variable cost is N$16 a bottle and its fixed costs are N$96 000 a month. Explain the difference between its contribution and its level of profit at that output.
items.canonical_answer: Contribution at an output is contribution per unit multiplied by the units sold - what the sales leave after their own variable costs. The level of profit is that figure after the fixed costs of the period have been taken off. At 12 000 bottles Kaoko's contribution is N$12 a bottle, or N$144 000, and its profit is N$48 000. The gap between the two is N$96 000, exactly the fixed costs, so the gap is the same whatever the output while both figures rise by N$12 with each extra bottle sold.

2 marks (AO2): applied to Kaoko - N$144 000 of contribution against N$48 000 of profit at 12 000 bottles, a gap equal to the N$96 000 of fixed costs; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: the two differ by exactly the fixed costs of the period.

items.prompt: Kaoko Juice sells 12 000 bottles at a contribution of N$12 each, with fixed costs of N$96 000 a month and a break-even output of 8 000. Calculate its monthly profit by two routes.
items.canonical_answer: Route one: profit = (contribution per unit x units sold) - fixed costs = (N$12 x 12 000) - N$96 000 = N$144 000 - N$96 000 = N$48 000. Route two: profit = margin of safety x contribution per unit = 4 000 x N$12 = N$48 000; the agreement between the routes is a check on the arithmetic. Interpreting the figure: Kaoko earns N$144 000 of contribution and keeps N$48 000 of it, a third, the other two thirds going to fixed costs. A month 20% below plan - 9 600 bottles - would give (N$12 x 9 600) - N$96 000 = N$19 200, which is 40% of the planned profit: a fifth off the volume takes 60% of the profit.
marking_guidance: Formula: profit = (contribution x units) - fixed costs, or margin of safety x contribution.
Substitution must be shown, not only the answer.
Units: the currency must appear on every figure.

Interpretation: must say what the profit means for the business - its size against contribution or its sensitivity to a fall in output. Agreement between the two routes is a check, not an interpretation.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of break-even analysis for a business.
items.canonical_answer: It assumes that everything produced is sold. Where a business builds stock it cannot shift, the revenue line on the chart shows income the business has not received, so the break-even point it reports is lower than the output the business actually has to sell. A firm working to that figure can believe it is trading profitably while unsold stock accumulates in the warehouse.
marking_guidance: The limitation must be developed - the limitation must be developed to a consequence for the business, not merely named.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of break-even analysis for a business that sells several different products.
items.canonical_answer: A single break-even chart assumes one product, or an unchanging mix between products. A business selling three things at different contributions has no single contribution per unit, so its break-even point moves whenever customers buy more of the low-contribution line and less of the high one - without any price or cost having changed. The figure can therefore be correct when it is calculated and wrong a month later for reasons the business never sees in its costs.
marking_guidance: The limitation must be developed - must reach why the figure moves for a multi-product business, not stop at 'it assumes one product'.

items.prompt: Analyse why break-even analysis is better suited to testing the effect of a proposed change than to predicting what a business's profit will be.
items.canonical_answer: The technique rests on assumptions - that all output is sold, that price holds at every volume, that variable cost per unit is constant. Used as a prediction, every one of those sits between the answer and reality, and each that fails moves the figure. Used to test a change, the calculation does something narrower and more reliable: it holds the other inputs still and shows the arithmetic effect of moving one, which tells the business how sensitive its position is to that input. What it does not do is settle which option is better, because the inputs held still may themselves respond - a price rise is proposed precisely because it changes revenue, and the same change may move volume. So the arithmetic isolates the effect, and the business finishes the comparison by asking which of the held-constant figures would not in fact hold.
marking_guidance: Condition: break-even rests on assumptions that may not hold.
Mechanism: holding other inputs constant isolates the effect of the one being changed.
Consequence: the technique measures sensitivity reliably and predicts unreliably.
Objective or stakeholder: must reach the quality of the decision the business makes with the figure.
Do not reward the claim that errors cancel out between two options.

items.prompt: A clothing manufacturer's finance director says break-even analysis is too simplistic to be worth using. Evaluate that view.
items.canonical_answer: It goes too far. The decisive criterion is what the business wants the technique to do: as a prediction of profit for a manufacturer selling many lines at different contributions, it is genuinely weak, because a single chart assumes a mix that will not hold and a price that will not hold either. But that is an argument for how to use it, not for abandoning it. The strongest case for the finance director is that a wrong number treated as reliable is worse than no number, and in a multi-product business the temptation to treat it as reliable is real. Against that, the manufacturer still needs to know how far a supplier increase moves the volume it must sell, and break-even answers that sensitivity question well. It does not by itself say the cheaper supplier is the better choice - that needs a judgement about whether quality, reliability or volume would move too. The judgement is that the technique should be kept for testing the sensitivity of single changes and individual lines, and not relied on as a forecast for the business as a whole.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation is required, not a balanced list.
Context: the answer must turn on this being a multi-product clothing manufacturer.
Criterion: the decisive test is what the business is asking the technique to do.
Counterargument: must give the genuine case for the finance director's view.
Condition: must state where the technique should and should not be used.

items.prompt: Otjiwa Dairy bottles one product. Price N$34 a litre; variable cost N$21 a litre; fixed costs N$139 100 a month. It sold 14 500 litres last month. Its supplier has announced a N$3 rise in the cost of packaging from next month, and the owner is considering raising the price to N$36. Calculate the current break-even output, margin of safety and profit; calculate what each becomes under the price rise with the higher packaging cost; and evaluate whether the owner should raise the price.
items.canonical_answer:
Now: contribution N$34 - N$21 = N$13. Break-even = N$139 100 / N$13 = 10 700 litres. Margin of safety = 14 500 - 10 700 = 3 800 litres (26.2%). Profit = (N$13 x 14 500) - N$139 100 = N$188 500 - N$139 100 = N$49 400.

With the N$3 cost rise and no price change: contribution N$10, break-even 13 910 litres, margin of safety 590 litres, profit N$5 900. With the price at N$36 as well: contribution N$36 - N$24 = N$12, break-even = 11 592 litres, margin of safety 2 908 litres, profit N$34 900 - all at the same 14 500 litres.

Judgement: raise the price. The decisive criterion is the margin of safety without it. Absorbing the whole N$3 leaves Otjiwa 590 litres from a loss - a margin of 4% - which is not a position a dairy with seasonal demand can hold. The rise restores it to 2 908 litres. The strongest argument against is that the whole calculation assumes 14 500 litres still sells at N$36, and it will not if buyers switch. The point where the price rise stops paying is where profit at N$12 contribution falls back to the N$5 900 it would earn without the rise: 12x - 139 100 = 5 900, so x = 12 083 litres - a loss of about 2 417 litres, or 17% of current volume. Below that loss the rise is still worth making; beyond it, it is not. The condition is therefore evidence about that response - what happened at the last price change, and what the nearest competitor charges. If neither is known, raising by less than the full N$2 and taking part of the cost on the margin is the safer course.
marking_guidance: All six figures must be calculated with working shown.
Judgement: the answer must recommend, not present both cases and stop.
Context: the recommendation must rest on Otjiwa's own margin of safety, not on the price rise in the abstract.
Criterion: the decisive factor is the margin of safety left if the cost is absorbed.
Counterargument: must address the assumption that volume holds at the higher price, with the indifference volume calculated, not estimated.
Condition: must name the evidence that would settle it.

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: Marula Foods makes three ready-meal lines in one factory. Under full costing the smallest line shows a loss of N$140 000 a year after taking its share of factory overheads; its contribution is N$310 000. Paragraph 2 - the mechanism if it stops: the contribution goes, the factory lease has four years to run so that overhead does not, and it is redistributed to the two remaining lines, whose recorded profit falls in turn. Paragraph 3 - the genuinely avoidable costs: the chiller is used by this line only, so its running cost and any dedicated labour would go; those belong in the calculation and the overhead share does not. Paragraph 4 - the strongest case for stopping: capacity and management attention freed for the two stronger lines, and a line permanently unable to cover its full share is being subsidised. items.prompt: Namib Signs prices its work at full cost plus 35%. Full cost is N$740 a sign, of which N$430 is variable. A government department offers a one-off order of 400 signs at N$560 each, for a month when the workshop is normally at 60% of its 1 500-sign capacity and has no other enquiries for the spare time. The order needs a one-off N$9 000 die to be cut. A regular commercial customer pays the full N$999. Analyse the circumstances under which Namib Signs should accept the order, and evaluate what it should do here.
items.canonical_answer:
On the numbers: at N$560 each sign leaves N$560 - N$430 = N$130, so 400 signs give N$52 000 of contribution, from which the N$9 000 die must be paid because it is incurred only for this order - leaving N$43 000. The workshop is at 60% of 1 500, so 600 signs of capacity are idle and the 400 fit with room to spare, with no enquiries waiting for that time. Under the cost-plus rule the order is N$439 below the usual price and looks like a loss of N$180 a sign against full cost; that comparison is the wrong one here, because the fixed element of the N$740 is paid whether the order is taken or not.

It should accept where three things hold: the capacity is genuinely idle, every cost the order itself causes is covered, and the price can be kept separate from the commercial list. It should refuse where the month fills with full-price work, because each sign would then displace N$569 of contribution rather than adding N$107 net of the die.

Recommendation: accept, as a one-off with the price documented as a tender for that contract only. The decisive factor is the idle capacity - N$43 000 that would otherwise not exist. The strongest argument against is visibility: government contract prices are often public, and the commercial customer paying N$999 may see it. That is why the recommendation is conditional on the order being genuinely one-off; if the department is likely to return annually, Namib Signs is setting a price rather than filling a gap, and should quote nearer full cost.
marking_guidance: Both the accept and the refuse circumstances must be analysed before recommending.
Judgement: a recommendation is required.
Context: must use the 60% capacity, the N$560 offer and the N$999 commercial price.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be whether the capacity is otherwise idle.
Counterargument: must address price visibility to the full-price customer.
Condition: must state what would reverse the recommendation.

items.prompt: A lender asks why it should trust the break-even figures in a business plan. Identify the questions you would ask about those figures before relying on them, and explain what each one tells you.
items.canonical_answer: Where did the price come from? A price taken from a competitor or a wish is weaker than one already being achieved. Where did the variable cost come from? Quoted, or estimated - and does it hold at the volume planned, or does it assume a bulk discount not yet agreed? Are all the fixed costs of the business in there, and is each one actually fixed? The test is how the amount behaves as output changes, not what the expense is called. An insurance premium and an annual accountancy retainer do not change with output, so they belong in the fixed total. Bank charges are usually a mixture: a monthly account fee is fixed, while charges levied per transaction rise with activity and belong with variable costs, so only the fixed part goes in the numerator. Anything genuinely fixed that is left out understates fixed costs and so understates the break-even output. Note that the owner's own drawings are not a business cost and do not belong in this calculation - they are a withdrawal of profit, and they belong in the cash-flow forecast, which answers a different question. Is everything produced assumed to be sold? If stock builds, the real figure is higher. Is this one product or several? A single chart across several products assumes a sales mix that will move. And how far above break-even is the plan? A margin of safety of a few per cent means the whole plan rests on estimates being right.
marking_guidance: State each question plainly before explaining it.
Give the reason each question matters - what a bad answer would mean for the figure.
Use the context: these are questions a lender asks about a plan, not about a trading business.
Classification must turn on how a cost behaves as output changes, not on the name of the expense; only the fixed part of a mixed charge belongs in the fixed-cost total.
Owner's drawings must be excluded from fixed costs and placed in the cash-flow forecast.

items.prompt: A manager refuses all work priced below the average cost per unit, saying it protects the business. Evaluate that policy.
items.canonical_answer: It is a reasonable default and a poor rule. The decisive criterion is whether the fixed costs inside the average actually change with the order: where capacity is idle they do not, so any price above variable cost adds to profit and the policy turns down money the business could have had. The strongest argument for the manager is that a rule is easy to apply consistently and hard to argue with, and a business that judges every order on contribution alone can drift into filling its capacity with thin work and never covering its fixed costs. The judgement is that the policy should be a starting point that a named person can override when capacity is genuinely spare and the price is documented as exceptional. It should stay firm when the business is near capacity, because then the average cost is much closer to the true cost of taking the work on.

items.prompt:
A single-product business's break-even chart is below. Identify the break-even level of output from it, and explain how you know the point you have chosen is the break-even point.

```
N$000        TR = total revenue      TC = total cost      FC = fixed costs
  480 |                                                    ***
      |                                                ****
  400 |                                           *****  +++++
      |                                       ****+++++++
  320 |                                ++**X**++
      |                       +++++++****
  240 |              +++++++++  *****
      |     +++++++++       ****
  160 |+++++-----------*****----------------------------------
      |            ****
   80 |       *****
      |   ****
    0 |***
      +---------+--------+--------+--------+--------+--------+>
      0       1 000    2 000    3 000    4 000    5 000    6 000  units
```

*Key: `*` is total revenue (TR), `+` is total cost (TC), `-` is fixed costs (FC), and `X` marks where TR and TC meet. All three lines are straight. TR passes through the origin; TC starts on the vertical axis at the level of the fixed cost line. Read values off the gridlines.*
items.canonical_answer: The two sloping lines meet at 4 000 units, so the break-even level of output is 4 000 units - read straight down from the meeting point to the horizontal axis. At that point both lines read N$320 000: total revenue exactly equals total cost, so the business makes neither a profit nor a loss. That is what identifies it. To the left the total cost line is above the revenue line and the vertical gap is a loss; to the right the revenue line is on top and the gap is profit. The fixed cost line at N$160 000 is not the break-even point, and it is worth being clear why. The revenue line does cross it, at 2 000 units - that is simply where sales have covered the fixed costs. But at 2 000 units total cost is N$160 000 of fixed costs plus N$80 000 of variable cost, or N$240 000, so revenue of N$160 000 there is still a loss of N$80 000. Break-even is where revenue meets TOTAL cost, not where it meets fixed costs.
marking_guidance: Comparison: the two sloping lines must be compared at the point where they meet.
Interpretation: the answer must say what the meeting means - revenue equal to total cost, so neither profit nor loss - and must distinguish it from the fixed cost line.
The output figure must be read from the chart, not calculated from figures given in the stem.

items.canonical_answer: At 6 000 units the revenue line reads N$480 000 and the total cost line reads N$400 000, so profit = N$480 000 - N$400 000 = N$80 000. Profit appears as the vertical gap between the two sloping lines, measured at the output in question and only to the right of where they meet. At 4 000 units the gap is zero; left of that the cost line is on top and the same gap is a loss. The gap widens by N$40 for every extra unit - the difference between the slopes of the two lines, which is the contribution per unit.

Reasoning: the mechanism is that profit is the vertical gap, and only right of the meeting point.

items.prompt: A printing business pays N$18 000 a month to rent its workshop, N$26 000 a month in salaries to three permanent staff, and N$4 a sheet for paper and ink. Identify whether each of these costs is fixed or variable, and explain what happens to each if the business prints nothing at all next month.
items.canonical_answer: The rent and the salaries are fixed costs: they do not change as output changes over the month, so the business still owes N$18 000 and N$26 000 - N$44 000 in all - even if it prints nothing. The paper and ink at N$4 a sheet is a variable cost, because it changes directly with output: print nothing and it is nothing, print 5 000 sheets and it is N$20 000. So a month with no printing still costs this business N$44 000, which is why the classification matters here - the fixed costs set the size of the hole that output has to fill.
marking_guidance: Context: must classify the N$18 000 rent, the N$26 000 salaries and the N$4 a sheet by name.
Reasoning: the reason a cost is fixed or variable is whether it changes as output changes, not what it is called.
Conclusion: must reach the N$44 000 still owed at zero output.

items.prompt: Explain how treating a variable cost as though it were fixed leads a business to the wrong total cost when output rises.
items.canonical_answer: Given that a cost has been put in the fixed total, it is carried into every calculation as one unchanging figure. When output rises, the mechanism is that the real cost rises with it while the recorded figure does not: total cost = fixed costs + variable cost per unit x output, so a cost left out of the per-unit term does not rise when output rises. The consequence is that recorded total cost rises more slowly than actual spending, so cost per unit looks as if it is falling faster than it is. For the business that reaches its profit: it believes each extra unit costs less than it does, so it may price too low or promise a margin it cannot deliver, and the gap widens the more it produces.
marking_guidance: Condition: the starting point is a variable cost recorded inside the fixed total.
Mechanism: because the fixed total is not multiplied by output, the rise in that cost is never picked up.
Consequence: the effect is an understated total cost that gets worse as output rises.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the profit of the business through pricing or margin.

items.prompt: A workshop has priced every job this year at variable cost plus N$30, using contribution costing. Its variable cost is N$70 a job, it completed 900 jobs, and its fixed costs for the year were N$32 000. Explain what this shows about the limitation of pricing on contribution alone.
items.canonical_answer: Each job earned N$30 of contribution, so 900 jobs earned 900 x N$30 = N$27 000 towards the fixed costs. The fixed costs were N$32 000, so the workshop ends the year N$5 000 short even though every single job was priced above its variable cost. That is the limitation: contribution costing leaves fixed costs out of the product figure, so a price that looks safe on every job can still fail to cover the year. The mark-up has to be set with the fixed total and the likely volume in view, and this is before the second problem - that the N$70 variable cost is assumed to hold at every volume, which overtime or a bulk discount would change.
marking_guidance: Context: must use the N$30 contribution, the 900 jobs and the N$32 000 of fixed costs.
Reasoning: the reason is that contribution costing excludes fixed costs from the product figure.
Conclusion: must reach the N$5 000 shortfall and what it means for setting the mark-up.

items.prompt: A Walvis Bay printing firm with spare machine time is offered a one-off order at a price above its variable cost per unit but below its full cost per unit. It is also considering opening a second print shop in Oshakati. Explain the difference between the decision that contribution costing suits and the one it does not.
items.canonical_answer: The difference is whether the decision changes the fixed costs. Contribution costing suits a short-run decision taken inside the existing cost structure: the one-off order uses spare machine time, and the firm's rent and salaries are the same whether it accepts or not, so an order priced above variable cost adds its contribution to profit even though it is below full cost - provided regular customers do not learn of the price and ask for it. It does not suit the second shop, whereas that decision brings new rent, staff and equipment, the fixed costs contribution costing sets aside, so the firm needs the full costs of the Oshakati shop set against the revenue it expects there.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - whether the decision leaves the fixed costs unchanged.

2 marks (AO2): applied to the firm - the one-off order using spare machine time, where fixed costs are the same either way, against the Oshakati shop, which brings new fixed costs; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: a short-run decision inside the existing cost structure against one that changes the fixed costs or sets a long-run price.

items.prompt: A Keetmanshoop brick maker makes 50 000 bricks a month at a total cost of N$150 000, of which N$60 000 is fixed. Each extra brick uses N$1.80 of clay, fuel and piece-rate wages. Explain the difference between its average cost and its marginal cost.
items.canonical_answer: Average cost is total cost divided by output - the share of the total each unit carries at that output, fixed costs included. Marginal cost is the cost of one more unit, which at AS is its variable cost. The brick maker's average cost is N$3.00 a brick and its marginal cost is N$1.80. The difference is what each measures - a total spread across units, whereas marginal cost is what one extra unit adds - not past against future, since both can be worked out from planned figures. So N$3.00 is the figure a long-run price has to cover, while an extra order at N$2.50 a brick still adds N$0.70 a brick to profit, provided there is spare capacity and the fixed costs do not rise.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - total cost spread across units at a stated output against the extra cost of one more unit.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the brick maker - N$3.00 a brick average against N$1.80 marginal, and what each tells it about a long-run price and an extra order; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: the difference is mathematical, not one of timing - do not reward past against future, since either can be calculated from planned figures.

items.prompt: A Windhoek craft brewery makes a bottle of beer for N$14 and adds a 50% mark-up. Similar local beers sell for N$24 to N$28, and its customers rate its beer above theirs. Explain the difference between setting its price from cost and setting it from the market.

Setting it from the market starts outside, with what customers will pay and what competitors charge, and cost then tests whether that price is worth supplying at. For the brewery, cost-plus gives N$21 a bottle, below every similar local beer although customers rate it higher, so if it would sell about as many at a higher price it leaves at least N$3 a bottle unclaimed. items.prompt: A school leaver is writing a plan for a car-wash and has worked out that it must wash 620 cars a month to break even. Explain what that figure gives her that a list of costs on its own does not.
items.canonical_answer: It gives her a target she can act on. The 620 is the number of washes at which her revenue would exactly equal her total costs, so she makes neither a profit nor a loss at that point; below it she is losing money and above it she is making some. A list of costs tells her what she will spend, but not how much work she has to find, because it says nothing about the price she charges or the volume she needs. Turning the same figures into 620 washes a month - about 21 a day - lets her ask the question that decides whether the plan is realistic: can she actually get 21 cars a day? That is why break-even analysis matters here; it converts the plan into a number she can test against the world.
marking_guidance: Context: must use the 620 figure and the fact that this is a plan, not a trading business.
Reasoning: the reason is that break-even converts costs and price into a required volume.
Conclusion: must reach what she can now do or test with the figure.

items.prompt: Explain how a thin margin of safety leads a business to change how it runs the next few months.
items.canonical_answer: The starting point is that the margin of safety is current output less break-even output, so where a business budgets 5 200 units against a break-even of 5 000, the margin is 200 units, or 200 / 5 200 = 3.8% of budgeted sales. The mechanism is that this is the whole of the room the forecast has: a shortfall of more than 3.8% in sales, or any rise in cost that lifts break-even output, puts the business into a loss rather than into a smaller profit. The consequence is that the plan cannot absorb an ordinary bad month, so the business has to act before one happens - watching sales weekly rather than at the year end, holding back discretionary spending that would raise fixed costs, or working on the price or the variable cost to pull break-even down. For the business that reaches survival as much as profit: a thin margin means there is no time to react after the fact.
marking_guidance: Condition: given a margin of safety that is a small percentage of budgeted output.
Mechanism: because the margin is the whole tolerance in the forecast, a small shortfall crosses into loss.
Consequence: the result is that the business must monitor and act earlier than it otherwise would.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the profit or survival of the business.

items.prompt: A bakery is deciding whether to raise the price of its loaves by 8%. Explain what break-even analysis can and cannot tell it before it decides.
items.canonical_answer: It can tell the bakery the arithmetic effect of the price rise on its own: a higher price per loaf raises contribution per loaf, which lowers the break-even output, so the bakery can see the new number of loaves it would need to sell to cover its costs. That is what break-even analysis is for here - testing the effect of a stated change before committing to it. What it cannot tell the bakery is the thing the decision turns on, which is how many loaves it will actually sell at the new price, because the analysis assumes everything produced is sold and that the selling price is the same at every volume. So the calculation gives the bakery the target it would have to hit; whether customers will still buy that many at the higher price is a judgement it has to make from what it knows about its customers and its competitors.
marking_guidance: Context: must use the 8% price rise and the bakery's decision.
Reasoning: the reason for the limit is the assumption that everything produced is sold at one price.
Conclusion: must reach what the bakery can and cannot decide on the figure.
